claim: 5-week-old male C57BL/6J Gria3-knockout mice (GluA3KO) and wild-type (GluA3WT) mice reared in ambient sound pressure level (SPL) of 55–75 dB had similar auditory brainstem response (ABR) thresholds.
source: GluA3KO and wild-type (GluA3WT) mice reared in ambient sound pressure level (SPL) of 55–75 dB had similar auditory brainstem response (ABR) thresholds, wave-1 amplitudes, and latencies.
evidence: The manuscript reports ABR measurements comparing GluA3KO and GluA3WT mice, with statistical analysis showing no significant differences in thresholds (F(1, 168) = 2.659, p = 0.11).

claim: 5-week-old male C57BL/6J Gria3-knockout mice (GluA3KO) and wild-type (GluA3WT) mice reared in ambient sound pressure level (SPL) of 55–75 dB had similar ABR wave-1 amplitudes.
source: GluA3KO and wild-type (GluA3WT) mice reared in ambient sound pressure level (SPL) of 55–75 dB had similar auditory brainstem response (ABR) thresholds, wave-1 amplitudes, and latencies.
evidence: The manuscript reports ABR wave-1 amplitude measurements with statistical analysis showing no significant differences between genotypes (F(1, 292) = 2.458, p = 0.118).

claim: 5-week-old male C57BL/6J Gria3-knockout mice (GluA3KO) and wild-type (GluA3WT) mice reared in ambient sound pressure level (SPL) of 55–75 dB had similar ABR wave-1 latencies.
source: GluA3KO and wild-type (GluA3WT) mice reared in ambient sound pressure level (SPL) of 55–75 dB had similar auditory brainstem response (ABR) thresholds, wave-1 amplitudes, and latencies.
evidence: The manuscript reports ABR wave-1 latency measurements with statistical analysis showing no significant differences between genotypes (F(1, 288) = 0.1273, p = 0.7215).

claim: Postsynaptic densities (PSDs) were larger on the modiolar side of the IHCs from GluA3WT.
source: Postsynaptic densities (PSDs), presynaptic ribbons, and synaptic vesicle sizes were all larger on the modiolar side of the IHCs from GluA3WT, but not GluA3KO, demonstrating GluA3 is required for modiolar–pillar synapse differentiation.
evidence: The manuscript reports ultrastructural measurements showing PSD surface areas were larger for modiolar-side synapses compared to pillar-side synapses in GluA3WT (p = 0.014 modiolar-1 vs. pillar, and p = 0.03 modiolar-2 vs. pillar).

claim: Presynaptic ribbons were larger on the modiolar side of the IHCs from GluA3WT.
source: Postsynaptic densities (PSDs), presynaptic ribbons, and synaptic vesicle sizes were all larger on the modiolar side of the IHCs from GluA3WT, but not GluA3KO, demonstrating GluA3 is required for modiolar–pillar synapse differentiation.
evidence: The manuscript reports that the surface area of modiolar-side ribbons was significantly larger (p = 0.002; modiolar mean: 0.141 ± 0.123 µm2; pillar mean: 0.074 ± 0.02 µm2) in GluA3WT.

claim: Synaptic vesicle sizes were larger on the modiolar side of the IHCs from GluA3WT.
source: Postsynaptic densities (PSDs), presynaptic ribbons, and synaptic vesicle sizes were all larger on the modiolar side of the IHCs from GluA3WT, but not GluA3KO, demonstrating GluA3 is required for modiolar–pillar synapse differentiation.
evidence: The manuscript reports that SVs of modiolar-side synapses were larger (p = 0.0029) than those of the pillar-side synapses (modiolar mean: 36 ± 3 nm; pillar mean: 33 ± 4 nm) in GluA3WT.

claim: Postsynaptic densities (PSDs) were not larger on the modiolar side of the IHCs from GluA3KO.
source: Postsynaptic densities (PSDs), presynaptic ribbons, and synaptic vesicle sizes were all larger on the modiolar side of the IHCs from GluA3WT, but not GluA3KO, demonstrating GluA3 is required for modiolar–pillar synapse differentiation.
evidence: The manuscript reports that PSD surface area comparison was not significant in GluA3KO (p = 0.67; modiolar-1 mean: 0.51 ± 0.18 µm2; modiolar-2 mean: 0.55 ± 0.14 µm2; pillar mean: 0.57 ± 0.16 µm2).

claim: GluA3 is required for modiolar–pillar synapse differentiation.
source: Postsynaptic densities (PSDs), presynaptic ribbons, and synaptic vesicle sizes were all larger on the modiolar side of the IHCs from GluA3WT, but not GluA3KO, demonstrating GluA3 is required for modiolar–pillar synapse differentiation.
evidence: The manuscript presents ultrastructural data showing modiolar-pillar differences in GluA3WT that are absent in GluA3KO, leading to the conclusion that GluA3 is required for this differentiation.

claim: Presynaptic ribbons juxtaposed with postsynaptic GluA2/4 subunits were similar in quantity between GluA3KO and GluA3WT.
source: Presynaptic ribbons juxtaposed with postsynaptic GluA2/4 subunits were similar in quantity, however, lone ribbons were more frequent in GluA3KO and GluA2-lacking synapses were observed only in GluA3KO.
evidence: The manuscript reports that paired synapses per IHC were similar in number for the whole cochlea (WT: 18.1 ± 2.8; KO: 17.3 ± 3.8; p = 0.94).

claim: Lone ribbons were more frequent in GluA3KO than in GluA3WT.
source: Presynaptic ribbons juxtaposed with postsynaptic GluA2/4 subunits were similar in quantity, however, lone ribbons were more frequent in GluA3KO and GluA2-lacking synapses were observed only in GluA3KO.
evidence: The manuscript reports that the numbers of lone ribbons per IHC (CtBP2-only) were significantly increased in GluA3KO relative to GluA3WT (WT: 0.97 ± 0.92; KO: 1.6 ± 0.84; p = 0.021).

claim: GluA2-lacking synapses were observed only in GluA3KO.
source: Presynaptic ribbons juxtaposed with postsynaptic GluA2/4 subunits were similar in quantity, however, lone ribbons were more frequent in GluA3KO and GluA2-lacking synapses were observed only in GluA3KO.
evidence: The manuscript reports that GluA2-lacking synapses per IHC (GluA4 + CtBP2) were significantly increased in GluA3KO (WT: 0.0 ± 0.0; KO: 0.07 ± 0.09; p = 0.028).

claim: GluA2 immunofluorescence volumes were smaller on the pillar side than the modiolar side in GluA3KO.
source: GluA2 and GluA4 immunofluorescence volumes were smaller on the pillar side than the modiolar side in GluA3KO, despite increased pillar-side PSD size.
evidence: The manuscript reports that in GluA3KO, GluA2 puncta were significantly larger on the modiolar side than the pillar side (p = 0.001 GluA2).

claim: GluA4 immunofluorescence volumes were smaller on the pillar side than the modiolar side in GluA3KO.
source: GluA2 and GluA4 immunofluorescence volumes were smaller on the pillar side than the modiolar side in GluA3KO, despite increased pillar-side PSD size.
evidence: The manuscript reports that in GluA3KO, GluA4 puncta were significantly larger on the modiolar side than the pillar side (p = 0.0001 GluA4).

claim: Pillar-side PSD size was increased in GluA3KO compared to GluA3WT.
source: GluA2 and GluA4 immunofluorescence volumes were smaller on the pillar side than the modiolar side in GluA3KO, despite increased pillar-side PSD size.
evidence: The manuscript reports that the mean surface area and volume of the pillar-side PSDs were larger in GluA3KO than GluA3WT (surface area: p = 0.013; volume: p = 0.007).

claim: The fluorescent puncta volumes of GluA2 were smaller in GluA3KO than GluA3WT.
source: Overall, the fluorescent puncta volumes of GluA2 and GluA4 were smaller in GluA3KO than GluA3WT.
evidence: The manuscript reports that the volumes of GluA2 puncta were significantly smaller in GluA3KO relative to GluA3WT (GluA2−GluA3WT: 0.47 ± 0.06; GluA2−GluA3KO: 0.39 ± 0.07, p = 0.0001).

claim: The fluorescent puncta volumes of GluA4 were smaller in GluA3KO than GluA3WT.
source: Overall, the fluorescent puncta volumes of GluA2 and GluA4 were smaller in GluA3KO than GluA3WT.
evidence: The manuscript reports that the volumes of GluA4 puncta were significantly smaller in GluA3KO relative to GluA3WT (GluA4−GluA3WT: 0.45 ± 0.05; GluA4−GluA3KO: 0.36 ± 0.02, p = 4.9e−6).

claim: GluA3KO contained less GluA2 immunofluorescence intensity relative to GluA3WT.
source: However, GluA3KO contained less GluA2 and greater GluA4 immunofluorescence intensity relative to GluA3WT (threefold greater mean GluA4:GluA2 ratio).
evidence: The manuscript reports that GluA2 intensity decreased in GluA3KO (GluA2 intensity (a.u.)e5 – GluA3WT: 1.8 ± 0.4; GluA3KO: 1.4 ± 0.3, p = 0.01).

claim: GluA3KO contained greater GluA4 immunofluorescence intensity relative to GluA3WT.
source: However, GluA3KO contained less GluA2 and greater GluA4 immunofluorescence intensity relative to GluA3WT (threefold greater mean GluA4:GluA2 ratio).
evidence: The manuscript reports that GluA4 intensity increased in GluA3KO (GluA4 intensity (a.u.)e5 – GluA3WT: 1.7 ± 0.6; GluA3KO: 4.2 ± 1.2, p = 5e−6).

claim: GluA3KO had a threefold greater mean GluA4:GluA2 ratio compared to GluA3WT.
source: However, GluA3KO contained less GluA2 and greater GluA4 immunofluorescence intensity relative to GluA3WT (threefold greater mean GluA4:GluA2 ratio).
evidence: The manuscript reports that the GluA4:GluA2 intensity ratio was 3× greater on average for GluA3KO synapses (GluA3WT: 0.93 ± 0.18; GluA3KO: 3.0 ± 0.5, p = 6e−7).

claim: GluA3 is essential in development, as germline disruption of Gria3 caused anatomical synapse pathology before cochlear output became symptomatic by ABR.
source: Thus, GluA3 is essential in development, as germline disruption of Gria3 caused anatomical synapse pathology before cochlear output became symptomatic by ABR.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing anatomical changes at 5 weeks of age when ABR is normal, combined with previous findings of ABR deficits at 8 weeks, supporting the conclusion that pathology precedes functional symptoms.

claim: The hearing loss in older male GluA3KO mice results from progressive synaptopathy evident in 5-week-old mice as decreased abundance of GluA2 subunits and an increase in GluA2-lacking, GluA4-monomeric Ca2+-permeable AMPARs.
source: We propose the hearing loss in older male GluA3KO mice results from progressive synaptopathy evident in 5-week-old mice as decreased abundance of GluA2 subunits and an increase in GluA2-lacking, GluA4-monomeric Ca2+-permeable AMPARs.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the observed changes in GluA2 and GluA4 subunit abundance at 5 weeks and previous findings of hearing loss at later ages.

claim: Cochlear sound encoding depends on α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazole propionic acid receptors (AMPARs).

claim: Gria3 disruption did not affect posttranscriptional flip and flop splicing of mRNA for GluA2 (Gria2 gene) or GluA4 (Gria4 gene) in the cochlea.
source: Thus, Gria3 disruption did not affect hearing sensitivity at 5 weeks of age, in contrast to 8 weeks of age when ABR peak amplitudes were reduced (García-Hernández et al., 2017). Taken together with previous work, this suggests the 5-week-old GluA3KO cochlea may be in a pathological but presymptomatic, vulnerable state. The levels of Gria2 or Gria4 flip or flop mRNA isoforms in cochleae of male mice at 5 weeks of age were similar in GluA3WT and GluA3KO.
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data showing no significant differences in flip or flop isoform levels between genotypes.

claim: In both GluA3WT and GluA3KO genotypes, expression of Gria2 and Gria4 flop isoforms appeared to exceed expression of the flip isoforms.

claim: Male GluA3KO mice have reduced ABR wave-1 amplitude relative to GluA3WT mice by 2 months of age (García-Hernández et al., 2017).

claim: Male GluA3KO mice have elevated ABR thresholds by 3 months of age (García-Hernández et al., 2017).

claim: In GluA3WT mice on C57BL/6 background, synapse components (ribbons, PSDs, and SVs) tended to be larger on the modiolar side.

evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data presented in Figure 8A.

claim: Non-GluA2 subunits preferentially heterodimerize with GluA2 subunits because homodimers are less stable energetically (Rossmann et al., 2011; Zhao et al., 2017).
source: Homodimers can form and homomeric tetramers may exist, but non-GluA2 subunits preferentially heterodimerize with GluA2 subunits because homodimers are less stable energetically (Rossmann et al., 2011; Zhao et al., 2017), suggesting that GluA2/4 heterodimers should be predominant in GluA3KO.

claim: Loss of GluA3 alters GluA2 and GluA4 subunit relative abundance, increasing the GluA4:GluA2 ratio.
source: However, we find that loss of GluA3 alters GluA2 and GluA4 subunit relative abundance, increasing the GluA4:GluA2 ratio (Figures 8D and 9D), which may increase the number of GluA2-lacking CP-AMPARs at cochlear ribbon synapses of the GluA3KO mice by forcing GluA4 homodimerization.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data presented in Figures 8D and 9D.

claim: The increase in GluA4:GluA2 ratio in GluA3KO may increase the number of GluA2-lacking CP-AMPARs at cochlear ribbon synapses by forcing GluA4 homodimerization.

evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observed changes in GluA2 and GluA4 abundance and known principles of AMPAR assembly.

claim: The increase in CP-AMPARs in the GluA3KO could make the IHC-ribbon synapses more vulnerable to excitotoxic noise trauma as the cochlea matures and ages.

claim: The duration of the postsynaptic current and thus the net influx of charge is largely determined by AMPAR desensitization, which is regulated by the proportion of flip and flop splice variants of GluA subunits (Sommer et al., 1990; Monyer et al., 1991; Mosbacher et al., 1994; Koike et al., 2000).

claim: Flip subunits desensitize more slowly than flop subunits, resulting in slower decays of AMPAR-mediated currents (Trussell and Fischbach, 1989; Lawrence and Trussell, 2000; Gardner et al., 2001; Quirk et al., 2004; Pei et al., 2007).

claim: In the inner ear in the absence of GluA3, flop isoforms of GluA2 and GluA4 were more abundant than flip isoforms, as in WT.

source: Pre- and postsynaptic ultrastructural features of IHC-ribbon synapses are disrupted in the organ of Corti of GluA3KO mice (Figures 3—5).

claim: The ultrastructure of endbulb synapses in the cochlear nucleus of GluA3KO mice is altered due to trans-synaptic developmental effects, where the absence of GluA3 increases synaptic depression by increasing the initial probability of vesicle release, slowing vesicle replenishment, and reducing the readily releasable pool of SVs through unknown mechanisms (García-Hernández et al., 2017; Antunes et al., 2020).
source: This is reminiscent of the ultrastructure of endbulb synapses in the cochlear nucleus of GluA3KO mice, which is altered due to trans-synaptic developmental effects, where the absence of GluA3 increases synaptic depression by increasing the initial probability of vesicle release, slowing vesicle replenishment, and reducing the readily releasable pool of SVs through unknown mechanisms (García-Hernández et al., 2017; Antunes et al., 2020).

claim: In the cochlea, modiolar–pillar ultrastructural differences among ribbon synapses were eliminated or reversed in GluA3KO.
source: In the cochlea, modiolar–pillar ultrastructural differences among ribbon synapses were eliminated or reversed in GluA3KO.

claim: The absence of GluA3 resulted in loss of the modiolar–pillar difference in PSD surface area seen in GluA3WT, due to larger PSDs on the pillar side of GluA3KO relative to GluA3WT.

source: Our ultrastructural data suggest that postsynaptic GluA3 subunits at IHC-ribbon synapses may perform an organizational function beyond their traditional role as ionotropic glutamate receptors.

claim: In GluA3KO, GluA2 and GluA4 puncta were significantly larger on the modiolar side than the pillar side.

claim: CtBP2 intensity increased in GluA3KO relative to GluA3WT.
source: In contrast to mean CtBP2 volume, which was decreased in GluA3KO (Figure 8A), median CtBP2 intensity (Figure 8B), and density (Figure 8C) were significantly increased in GluA3KO. For CtBP2 intensity (a.u.)e5 – GluA3WT: 1.2 ± 0.3; GluA3KO: 1.8 ± 0.3, p = 0.0001.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence intensity measurements presented in Figure 8B.

claim: GluA2 intensity and volume were both reduced in GluA3KO, resulting in no change in GluA2 density.
source: As shown in the representative images assessed in Figure 7, GluA2 intensity and volume were both reduced (Figure 8A, B), resulting in no change in GluA2 density (Figure 8C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence measurements presented in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: While GluA4 intensity increased, volume was reduced in GluA3KO, resulting in increased GluA4 density.
source: While GluA4 intensity increased, volume was reduced (Figure 8A, B), resulting in increased GluA4 density (Figure 8C).

claim: Relative to GluA3WT synapses, the GluA4:GluA2 intensity ratio was 3× greater on average for GluA3KO synapses.

claim: Increases of the GluA4:GluA2 intensity ratios in GluA3KO relative to GluA3WT tended to be greater for synapses on the pillar side than the modiolar side.

claim: Synapse alterations in GluA3KO were greatest on the pillar side, suggesting defective molecular differentiation of synapse properties along the morphological modiolar–pillar axis.
